1-foundation.title: Comparing antiseptics
1-foundation.stem: Students use a teacher-approved bacterial culture on agar. Equal paper discs contain antiseptic A, antiseptic B or sterile water. Mean clear-zone diameters are A: 12 mm; B: 8 mm; water: 0 mm.

parts.q: Explain why the agar and inoculating equipment should be sterile.
ms: Sterilisation removes unwanted microorganisms.
This reduces contamination so growth reflects the intended bacterial culture.

parts.q: Give two controlled variables, other than disc size.
ms: Use the same bacterial species / starting concentration.
Keep agar depth, incubation temperature or incubation time the same (one additional valid control).

parts.q: Use π = 3.14 to calculate the area of A’s clear circular zone.
ms: Radius = 12/2 = 6 mm.
Area = πr² = 3.14 × 36.
Area = 113.04 mm².

parts.q: State a conclusion, its supporting evidence, and one reason to repeat the investigation.
ms: A inhibits growth more than B under the tested conditions.
A has a larger clear zone than B; the water control has none.
Repeats allow a mean and identification of variation / anomalous results.

1-foundation.title: Investigating yellow leaves
1-foundation.stem: Tomato plants have yellow leaves and slow growth. No pathogen has yet been identified. Group 1 receives a complete mineral solution; group 2 receives an identical solution without magnesium. All other conditions are kept equal.

parts.q: Explain why a yellow leaf does not by itself prove infection.
ms: Several conditions can cause yellowing.
A mineral deficiency rather than a pathogen may be responsible.

parts.q: Explain why lacking magnesium can reduce growth.
ms: Magnesium is required for chlorophyll production.
Less chlorophyll reduces light absorption / photosynthesis.
Less glucose is available to make biomass / support growth.

parts.q: State three controls for the comparison.
ms: Use the same plant species and similar starting age / size.
Provide the same light and temperature (one valid environmental control).
Provide equal solution volumes and all other mineral concentrations.

parts.q: Suggest a useful additional diagnostic method and explain its purpose.
ms: Use a suitable laboratory test / pathogen identification or validated antibody test.
It can identify or provide evidence of a particular pathogen rather than relying on symptoms alone.

1-foundation.title: Defending plants
1-foundation.stem: A leaf-eating mammal attacks plants with soft leaves. A second plant has thorns and contains a toxic chemical. A third plant has damaged bark and a fungal infection.

parts.q: Explain how thorns and a toxic chemical can reduce damage.
ms: Thorns can deter or injure herbivores, reducing feeding.
Toxic chemicals can poison / deter herbivores.
Reduced feeding preserves tissues needed for growth / photosynthesis.

parts.q: Describe two physical barriers, other than thorns, and explain one of their effects.
ms: Cellulose cell walls provide a physical barrier.
Waxy cuticle or bark provides another physical barrier.
A barrier reduces pathogen entry into plant tissues.

parts.q: Explain why bark damage can increase infection risk.
ms: Damage breaches a physical barrier.
Fungal pathogens can enter exposed tissues more easily.

parts.q: Give two ways a plant can defend itself after infection or attack.
ms: Produce antibacterial chemicals / defensive poisons.
Shed infected leaves or use another valid specified defence such as curling leaves.

1-higher.title: Assessing an antiseptic claim
1-higher.stem: An antiseptic company compares equal discs on agar seeded with one approved bacterial strain. Mean inhibition diameters are control: 6 mm; low concentration: 10 mm; high concentration: 14 mm. All discs are 6 mm wide. The company claims its product kills every type of pathogen.

parts.q: Calculate the clear-zone area outside the high-concentration disc, using π = 3.14.
ms: Outer radius = 7 mm and disc radius = 3 mm.
Subtract areas: π(7² − 3²).
Area = 125.6 mm².

parts.q: Explain why the claim is not justified.
ms: Only one bacterial strain was tested, not every pathogen.
Inhibition of visible growth does not prove all cells were killed.
The claim extends beyond the experimental conditions / ignores viruses, fungi or other untested pathogens.

parts.q: Describe two precautions that reduce contamination and one school incubation precaution.
ms: Sterilise medium / equipment.
Open lids briefly and use aseptic inoculation.
Incubate at 25°C and do not reopen incubated plates.

parts.q: Why report several independent plates rather than a single plate?
ms: To assess variation and improve reliability of a mean.

1-higher.title: Targeted antibody delivery
1-higher.stem: A tumour has antigen X on many of its cells. Scientists make a monoclonal antibody against X and attach a drug. In a trial, 42 of 70 treated patients improve, compared with 21 of 70 receiving the comparison treatment.

parts.q: Describe how a hybridoma producing the antibody is made.
ms: Expose a mouse to the antigen and obtain antibody-producing lymphocytes.
Fuse lymphocytes with tumour cells.
Select and clone a suitable hybridoma to produce identical antibodies.

parts.q: Explain the advantage of attaching the drug to this antibody.
ms: The antibody binds specifically to antigen X.
Attached drug is delivered to antigen-bearing target cells.
This may reduce exposure / damage to healthy cells compared with non-targeted delivery.

parts.q: Calculate the difference in improvement percentage points.
ms: Comparison: 21/70 × 100 = 30%.
Difference = 30 percentage points.

parts.q: Give one reason the improvement data alone do not establish that the treatment is preferable.
ms: Side effects, long-term outcome, cost or comparable trial design must also be evaluated.

1-higher.title: Diagnosing a crop problem
1-higher.stem: A crop has yellow leaves. Some plants also have black spots. An agronomist compares magnesium content, performs a pathogen test and investigates whether spraying a fungicide improves growth.

parts.q: Distinguish two possible causes of yellow leaves and explain a growth effect.
ms: Magnesium deficiency can reduce chlorophyll.
A pathogen can damage photosynthetic tissue.
Either can reduce photosynthesis and glucose available for growth.

parts.q: Explain why a positive pathogen test does not prove every yellow leaf is caused only by that pathogen.
ms: The test identifies presence / a marker, not all causes of every symptom.
Mineral deficiency or other environmental causes may coexist.

parts.q: Design a controlled comparison of the fungicide’s effect.
ms: Randomly allocate similar affected plants to fungicide and control groups.
Keep nutrient supply, light, water and other conditions constant.
Repeat with enough plants and compare mean growth using the same measurement interval.

parts.q: Explain how an intact cuticle and a defensive chemical can help plants.
ms: A cuticle reduces pathogen entry as a physical barrier.
A defensive chemical can inhibit microbes or deter herbivores.

2-foundation.title: Focusing on a book
2-foundation.stem: A student looks from a distant tree to a nearby book. Light must be focused on the retina. Another student is short-sighted: distant light focuses in front of the retina.

parts.q: State the functions of the retina and optic nerve.
ms: The retina contains light-sensitive receptors.
The optic nerve carries impulses from the eye to the brain.

parts.q: Describe how the eye accommodates to the nearby book.
ms: Ciliary muscles contract.
Suspensory ligaments loosen.
The lens becomes thicker / refracts light more strongly.

parts.q: State how pupil size changes in bright light and explain its benefit.
ms: The pupil becomes smaller.
Less light enters, protecting the light-sensitive retina.

parts.q: Name the correcting lens for short sight and explain where corrected light should focus.
ms: Use a concave lens.
It refracts the light so the final image is focused on the retina.

parts.q: Give one alternative to spectacles for correcting a vision defect.
ms: Contact lenses, appropriate laser surgery or lens replacement.

2-foundation.title: Treating kidney failure
2-foundation.stem: A patient with kidney failure receives dialysis three times a week. A possible transplant would require a donor and medicines to reduce rejection.

parts.q: Name the organ that produces urea and the organ that removes it from blood.
ms: Urea is produced in the liver.
Kidneys remove it from blood.

parts.q: Name two useful substances normally reabsorbed by kidneys after filtration.
ms: Glucose.
An appropriate amount of water or ions.

parts.q: Describe the basic action of dialysis.
ms: Blood passes alongside dialysis fluid separated by a partially permeable membrane.
Urea moves from blood into dialysis fluid down a concentration gradient.
Blood cells and large proteins are retained.

parts.q: Compare a transplant with continuing dialysis.
ms: A successful transplant can give continuous function / avoid repeated dialysis sessions.
It requires a donor and has surgical / rejection risks.
Immune-suppressing medicines reduce rejection but increase infection risk.

2-foundation.title: Light and seedling growth
2-foundation.stem: Ten similar seedlings receive light from the left. Ten controls receive light equally from all sides. Both groups receive the same water, temperature and growing medium. After four days, shoots in the first group bend left.

parts.q: Name this directional growth response and explain the word positive.
ms: Phototropism.
Positive means growth towards the light stimulus.

parts.q: Explain why the evenly lit control group is useful.
ms: It provides a comparison without directional lighting.
A difference can therefore be linked more confidently to light direction.

parts.q: Give two measurements or records that improve the investigation.
ms: Measure shoot length / change in length.
Record direction using accurate labelled drawings or a consistent angle measure.

parts.q: Explain how plant hormones can cause bending.
ms: Unequal hormone / auxin distribution develops across the shoot.
The two sides grow at different rates.

parts.q: State the usual growth response of a root and shoot to gravity.
ms: Roots grow towards gravity / positive gravitropism.
Shoots grow against gravity / negative gravitropism.

2-higher.title: Keeping warm and conserving water
2-higher.stem: A runner finishes training in cold dry air. Core temperature falls slightly and blood becomes more concentrated because water has been lost. No water is drunk immediately.

parts.q: Explain how shivering and vasoconstriction oppose the temperature fall.
ms: Shivering involves repeated muscle contraction and increased respiration.
Energy is transferred to thermal stores.
Vasoconstriction reduces blood flow near the skin.
This reduces energy transfer to the surroundings.

parts.q: Explain the ADH response to the more concentrated blood.
ms: A change in blood water concentration is detected in the brain.
The pituitary releases more ADH.
Kidney tubules become more permeable to water.
More water is reabsorbed into blood, producing a smaller volume of concentrated urine.

parts.q: Explain why this is negative feedback.
ms: The responses oppose the original change in water concentration.
As conditions return towards normal, the corrective ADH signal decreases.

2-higher.title: Researching a brain injury
2-higher.stem: A patient has impaired balance after a brain injury. MRI shows damage near the cerebellum. Researchers consider electrical stimulation during a clinically necessary procedure.

parts.q: State the normal function of the cerebellum and explain one limitation of linking the scan to the symptom.
ms: The cerebellum coordinates movement / balance.
Connected pathways may also be affected, so the symptom does not isolate one region’s function.

parts.q: Evaluate electrical stimulation as evidence for brain function.
ms: A reproducible response can link activation of a region to a function.
Complex connections mean stimulation may influence other regions.
Delicate brain tissue creates a risk of irreversible harm.
Informed consent and likely clinical benefit must justify the procedure.

parts.q: The patient looks from a near object to a distant one. Explain accommodation.
ms: Ciliary muscles relax.
Suspensory ligaments tighten.
The lens is pulled thinner.
It refracts light less strongly to focus the distant object on the retina.

2-higher.title: Assessing food-production choices
2-higher.stem: A farm’s feed contains 6000 kg dry biomass and its livestock gain 480 kg dry biomass. A proposed system reduces animal movement and controls temperature. The farm also considers replacing part of its output with fungal mycoprotein.

parts.q: Calculate biomass transfer efficiency.
ms: Efficiency = gain / input × 100.

parts.q: Explain two reasons the remaining input biomass does not become new livestock biomass.
ms: Some food is not digested and is egested.
Some absorbed material is lost through respiration / excretion, such as carbon dioxide, water or urea.

parts.q: Explain how the proposed livestock system could increase yield and give one drawback.
ms: Less movement reduces energy transferred in muscle activity.
Controlled temperature reduces energy demand for keeping warm.
A valid drawback concerns welfare, disease, cost or resource use.

parts.q: Explain one requirement for producing fungal mycoprotein and evaluate a potential benefit and limitation.
ms: A suitable carbohydrate supply, oxygen for aerobic growth or controlled temperature supports fungal growth in fermenters.
A valid benefit includes protein production with potentially less livestock demand.
A limitation such as energy / input costs, environmental impacts or consumer acceptance must be considered.
